title: Vetala Extended Tale 88: The King Who Judged His Own Son

full_text:
The king hoisted the Vetala again. The corpse began:

"The crown prince of Avanti, driving his chariot recklessly through the crowded market, struck and killed the only son of an impoverished weaver woman. The weaver woman ran into the royal court, weeping and holding the corpse of her child, demanding justice.

The royal counselors urged the king: 'Pay the woman ten thousand gold coins; she is a pauper and can live in luxury. You cannot execute the only heir to the dynasty for a peasant.'

King Vikramaditya of the tale stepped down from his golden throne, stripped the prince of his royal garments, ordered him tried before the public court, and paid the imperial blood penalty from his personal fortune while exiling the prince to serve as a humble laborer in the weaver's guild until the debt of sorrow was repaid.

Tell me, Vikram: did the king weaken the throne by punishing his own flesh?"

King Vikramaditya answered: "He made the throne immortal. A kingdom survives not by dynastic blood, but by unyielding justice. When a king proves that no rank, wealth, or royal birth can shield an offender from the law, the people place their absolute faith in the crown, creating an unshakeable empire of dharma."

"Spoken like the true King of Ujjayini!" laughed the Vetala, and darted away.
moral: A ruler who places his own blood above the law forfeits the right to govern his people.
